concepts.title: Equality as a Foundational Ideal of Political Theory

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Equality as a Foundational Ideal of Political Theory' refers to.
questions.a: Equality does not claim that all people are identical in talent or taste; it claims that every person deserves the same consideration and respect simply as a human being. Because humans alone can reason about their actions and speak for their interests, political theory treats equal moral worth as the starting point of justice.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Equality as a Foundational Ideal of Political Theory'.
questions.a: Difference in ability is not a licence for difference in dignity -- equal consideration is owed to every person.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Equality as a Foundational Ideal of Political Theory' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: keps101.txt lines 1-90 (introduction, human uniqueness of reason and language, equality as basic premise of political theory))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Natural and Social Inequalities' refers to.
questions.a: Some inequalities arise from inborn differences of strength, intelligence or talent -- natural inequalities -- while others are manufactured by society through unequal access to wealth, education and power -- social inequalities. Political theory worries mainly about the second kind, since they are humanly created and can therefore be humanly removed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Natural and Social Inequalities'.
questions.a: Born differences need not become social hierarchies -- the arrangements we build decide whether they do.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Natural and Social Inequalities' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps101.txt lines 90-170 (distinction between natural and social inequalities, examples of caste and gender hierarchy, whether inequalities are inevitable))

concepts.title: Three Dimensions of Equality: Political, Social and Economic

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Three Dimensions of Equality: Political, Social and Economic' refers to.
questions.a: Equality operates on three linked fronts. Political equality grants each adult an equal vote and equal right to hold office; social equality rejects status hierarchies of caste, religion and gender in everyday life; economic equality asks that wealth differences not be so extreme that they swallow the other two.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Three Dimensions of Equality: Political, Social and Economic'.
questions.a: One vote and one law mean little if caste still stigmatises or wealth still commands -- the three equalities need each other.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Three Dimensions of Equality: Political, Social and Economic' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps101.txt lines 170-260 (dimensions of equality, political social and economic equality, why formal equality alone is insufficient))

concepts.title: Equality of Opportunity and Natural Rights

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Equality of Opportunity and Natural Rights' refers to.
questions.a: Equality of opportunity demands that positions and prizes go to effort and talent rather than birth, which requires at least a fair starting line for all. The related liberal claim of natural rights holds that every person possesses certain rights -- life, liberty and the like -- before and above any government, which no ruler may cancel.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Equality of Opportunity and Natural Rights'.
questions.a: Fair competition needs fair starting points, and rights that precede the state protect the competitor.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Equality of Opportunity and Natural Rights' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.4 (source: keps101.txt lines 260-350 (equality of opportunity, affirmative action debate, natural rights and their role in liberal thought))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Equality in the Indian Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution weaves equality through its fabric: Articles 14 to 18 promise equality before law, ban untouchability and titles, and guarantee equal public access; Article 15 and 16 permit special provisions for disadvantaged groups; and directive principles push toward reducing economic concentration.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Equality in the Indian Constitution'.
questions.a: Formal equality plus enabling provisions for the disadvantaged -- the Constitution treats equality as a project, not just a rule.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Equality in the Indian Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.5 (source: keps101.txt lines 350-430 (equality provisions of the Indian constitution, Articles 14 to 18, provisions for disadvantaged groups and reservations))
